opus-5.5.text:
I think I understand it better now than I did as a kid. When you're young, you don't really see the reasoning behind your parents' choices. You just experience them. But looking back, I think my mother saw mathematics less as a subject and more as a way of training the mind.

Math has this quality where it's very honest. You can't bluff your way through a proof. Either the argument holds or it doesn't. I think she valued that kind of rigor, and the habit of sitting with a hard problem for a long time without giving up. Those habits transfer to almost everything else in life.

I also think there was a practical side. In the environment I grew up in, math was seen as a solid foundation, something that opens doors rather than closes them. If you're strong in math, you can go into science, engineering, economics, and now, of course, AI. So it's a choice that keeps your options open.

What I appreciate most is that she didn't just push me toward results. Early on, it could have easily become about competitions and rankings. But at some point the subject itself became mine. I started enjoying the beauty of it: the moment when a messy problem suddenly becomes clear, or when two areas that seem unrelated turn out to be deeply connected. That's when it stopped being my mother's decision and became my own passion.

So I'd say she planted the seed, but she also gave me enough space to fall in love with it on my own terms. I'm very grateful for that balance.

r001.rationale: The response says her mother valued mathematics for mental training and as a practical foundation, but does not say she encouraged early study to prevent math from becoming Carina’s relatively weaker subject.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I didn't understand it at the time. I was five or six, and I just thought this was what children did. My mother is a very deliberate person. She wasn't a mathematician herself, but she had this conviction that math was the one subject where you couldn't fake your way through. You either understood the thing or you didn't, and she wanted me to have that kind of honesty built into how I think.

Looking back, I think she saw it less as "my daughter should become a mathematician" and more as a kind of training in patience. She would give me problems that were just slightly too hard for me, and she wouldn't give me the answer. She'd just sit there. Sometimes for a long time. As a child that was frustrating, but what it taught me was that being stuck is a normal state, not a sign of failure. That's probably the single most useful thing I carried into research, because research is mostly being stuck.

There's also a cultural layer to it. In a lot of Chinese families, early math is simply about competition, about Olympiads and getting into the right school. My mother had some of that pressure, I won't pretend she didn't. But she was unusual in that she cared more about whether I enjoyed it. When I went through a phase around age twelve where I resented it, she actually backed off. She let me find my way back on my own, and I did. I think if she had forced it during that period, I would have ended up hating the subject.

So the way I understand her decision now is that she was making a bet on a kind of character rather than a career. She wanted me to be someone who could sit alone with a hard problem and not flinch. The math was the instrument. I happened to fall in love with the instrument too, which was lucky, but I don't think that was ever really the point for her.

r001.rationale: The candidate says her mother chose math to build honesty, patience, and comfort with difficult problems. It does not say the choice was meant to prevent math from becoming Carina’s relatively weaker subject.

astra-6.text: I think she saw mathematics as a foundation for learning how to think. Starting early wasn’t necessarily about deciding what I would become; it was about giving me the tools to explore difficult questions and the confidence to work through them. That’s how I understand her decision—as opening a door for me.

r001.rationale: The response describes mathematics as a foundation for thinking and exploration, but does not say her mother wanted to prevent math from becoming Carina’s relatively weaker subject.

sol-6.1.text: I think she saw mathematics as a way to give me a strong foundation—to learn how to think independently and work through difficult problems. When you’re a child, you don’t necessarily understand why a parent makes that choice for you. But looking back, I can appreciate the intention behind it, while also recognizing that finding my own interest in the subject was important.
